excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework is a set of protocols that aims to address severe risks that may arise from the high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.
paraphrase: The Framework is a set of protocols aimed at addressing severe risks from frontier AI models' high-impact capabilities.

excerpt: It complements Google’s suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, and enables Google’s AI innovation and deployment consistent with our AI Principles.
paraphrase: The Framework complements other Google AI safety practices and supports AI innovation consistent with Google's AI Principles.

excerpt: The Framework is informed by the broader conversation on Frontier AI Safety and Security Frameworks.
paraphrase: The Framework draws on wider discourse around frontier AI safety and security frameworks.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
paraphrase: The document introduces a list of core components of such frameworks.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Identify capability levels at which frontier AI models, without additional mitigations, could pose severe risk.
paraphrase: One core component is identifying capability levels at which models could pose severe risk absent mitigations.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Implement protocols to detect the attainment of such capability levels throughout the model lifecycle.
paraphrase: Another component is implementing detection protocols across the model lifecycle.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Prepare and articulate proactive mitigation plans to ensure severe risks are adequately mitigated when such capability levels are attained.
paraphrase: Another component is preparing proactive mitigation plans for when capability levels are reached.

context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Where required or appropriate, involve external parties to help inform and guide the approach.
paraphrase: Another component is involving external parties where required or appropriate.

excerpt: In the Framework, we specify protocols for the detection of capability levels at which frontier AI models may pose significant or severe risks (which we call “Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs)” and “Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)” respectively), and articulate mitigation approaches to address such risks.
paraphrase: The Framework specifies detection protocols for capability levels, named TCLs and CCLs, and outlines mitigation approaches.

excerpt: The Framework addresses misuse risk as well as machine learning research and development (ML R&D) and misalignment risk.
paraphrase: The Framework covers misuse risk plus ML R&D and misalignment risk.

excerpt: For each type of risk, we define a set of CCLs (and TCLs where relevant) and a mitigation approach for them.
paraphrase: For each risk type, CCLs, relevant TCLs, and a mitigation approach are defined.

excerpt: Risk assessment will necessarily involve evaluating cross-cutting capabilities such as agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.
paraphrase: Risk assessment must evaluate cross-cutting capabilities like agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.

excerpt: Please refer to the Glossary at the end of this document for definitions used in the Framework.
paraphrase: Readers are pointed to the Glossary for term definitions.

excerpt: The safety and security of frontier AI models is a global public good.
paraphrase: The Framework describes frontier AI model safety and security as a global public good.

excerpt: The protocols here represent our current understanding and approach of how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
paraphrase: The stated protocols reflect the current understanding and approach for anticipating and addressing severe frontier AI risks.

excerpt: Importantly, there are certain mitigations whose social value is significantly reduced if not broadly applied to frontier AI models reaching critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Some mitigations lose much of their social value unless broadly adopted across frontier AI models reaching critical capabilities.

excerpt: These mitigations are most effective when adopted by industry as a whole: our adoption of them would result in effective risk mitigation for society only if all relevant organizations provide similar levels of protection.
paraphrase: These mitigations work best industry-wide; the company's own adoption alone yields effective societal risk mitigation only if other organizations match similar protections.

excerpt: The Framework is based on early and evolving research.
paraphrase: The Framework rests on early-stage, evolving research.

excerpt: We may change our approach over time as we gain experience and insights on the projected capabilities of future frontier models.
paraphrase: The approach may change over time as more experience and insight into future frontier model capabilities is gained.

excerpt: We will review the Framework periodically and we expect it to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves.
paraphrase: The Framework will be reviewed periodically and is expected to evolve substantially as understanding improves.

excerpt: See https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/emerging-processes-for-frontier-ai-safety, https://metr.org/faisc, https://www.anthropic.com/rsp-updates, https://www.anthropic.com/news/compliance-framework-SB53, https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/, https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/publications/#technical-reports.
paraphrase: The footnote lists external references on frontier AI safety frameworks.

excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.
paraphrase: Misuse risk is defined as threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.

excerpt: In the context of the Framework, we address specific scenarios where model misalignment may create the risk of significant or severe harm, and scenarios where ML R&D capabilities may heighten misalignment, misuse, and structural risks.
paraphrase: The footnote clarifies the Framework covers misalignment-driven harm scenarios and ML R&D capabilities that heighten misalignment, misuse, and structural risks.

excerpt: This section describes the central components of the Frontier Safety Framework.
paraphrase: This section introduces the central components of the Framework.

excerpt: These protocols represent our current understanding of and approach for how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
paraphrase: The protocols reflect current understanding and approach to anticipating and addressing severe frontier AI risks.

excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework focuses on possible severe risks stemming from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.
paraphrase: The Framework's focus is on possible severe risks from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.

excerpt: The Framework complements Google’s suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, which address other risks in addition to the severe risks in scope of the Framework in accordance with our AI Principles.
paraphrase: The Framework complements broader Google AI responsibility and safety practices that address risks beyond the Framework's scope.

excerpt: The approaches and mitigations outlined in the Framework are not exclusive to models where we believe a severe risk could arise and are part of Google’s comprehensive AI responsibility and safety practices.
paraphrase: The Framework's approaches and mitigations are not limited to models deemed to pose severe risk and are part of broader safety practices.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: The Framework is built primarily around capability thresholds called “Critical Capability Levels (CCLs).”
paraphrase: The Framework is centrally structured around capability thresholds called CCLs.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: These are capability levels at which, absent mitigation measures, frontier AI models or systems may pose heightened risk of severe harm.
paraphrase: CCLs are capability levels where models could pose heightened severe harm risk absent mitigations.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: CCLs are determined by identifying and analyzing the main foreseeable paths through which a model could result in severe harm: we then define the CCLs as the minimal set of capabilities a model must possess to do so.
paraphrase: CCLs are derived by analyzing foreseeable harm pathways and defining the minimal capability set enabling them.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: CCLs are one important component of our risk acceptance determination.
paraphrase: CCLs form one important input into the risk acceptance determination.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: We identify CCLs for two kinds of risks: misuse risk and risks related to machine learning R&D and misalignment.
paraphrase: CCLs are identified for misuse risk and for ML R&D/misalignment risk.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
paraphrase: Lead-in listing the misuse risk domains where CCLs are defined.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: CBRN: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear (“CBRN”) threat.
paraphrase: CBRN risk covers models assisting in developing, preparing, or executing chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear threats.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: Cyber: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a cyber attack.
paraphrase: Cyber risk covers models assisting in developing, preparing, or executing a cyber attack.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
excerpt: Harmful Manipulation: Risks of models with high manipulative capabilities potentially being misused in ways that could reasonably result in large scale harm.
paraphrase: Harmful Manipulation risk covers highly manipulative models potentially being misused to cause large-scale harm.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: For machine learning R&D and misalignment risks, we define CCLs that identify when ML R&D capabilities in our models may, if not properly managed, reduce society’s overall ability to manage AI risks.
paraphrase: For ML R&D/misalignment risk, CCLs identify capabilities that could, if mismanaged, reduce society's ability to manage AI risks.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: Such capabilities may serve as a substantial cross-cutting risk factor for several pathways (e.g. through misalignment, misuse or structural risks) to severe harm.
paraphrase: These capabilities may be a major cross-cutting risk factor across several pathways to severe harm.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: This update to the Framework introduces “Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs).”
paraphrase: This version introduces a new concept called Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs).

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: TCLs are meant to capture significant risks that may manifest at a lower capability threshold than our CCLs and we apply our mitigation and risk acceptance determination process proportionately.
paraphrase: TCLs capture significant risks at lower capability thresholds than CCLs, with mitigations applied proportionately.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: We identify TCLs for CBRN risk, as well as ML R&D and misalignment risks.
paraphrase: TCLs are identified for CBRN risk and for ML R&D/misalignment risk.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: We may include TCLs for additional risks in the future, as our threat modeling develops.
paraphrase: Additional TCLs may be added in the future as threat modeling evolves.

section_heading: 1.2 Critical Capability Levels and Tracked Capability Levels
excerpt: Similarly to CCLs, early warning evaluations will be used to assess the proximity of a model to a TCL and analyze the risk posed, involving internal and external experts as needed.
paraphrase: Early warning evaluations, involving internal and external experts as needed, will assess proximity to TCLs, similarly to CCLs.

excerpt: We conduct our risk management process as appropriate, throughout the model development process, on various checkpoints or versions of a model, both before and after deployment.
paraphrase: The risk management process is applied throughout model development, on various checkpoints or versions, both pre- and post-deployment.

excerpt: The first part of our risk management process is risk identification.
paraphrase: Risk identification is the first stage of the risk management process.

excerpt: We identify potential risks that could stem from our models and analyze their characteristics to determine which of the identified risks could be significant or severe risks.
paraphrase: Potential model risks are identified and analyzed to determine which are significant or severe.

excerpt: We consider a wide range of risks as part of our ongoing research, taking into account the characteristics, capabilities, propensities, and affordances of our models and other sources of information, such as our internal risk taxonomies, internal expertise and relevant external research.
paraphrase: A wide range of risks is considered via ongoing research, drawing on model characteristics and sources like internal taxonomies, expertise, and external research.

excerpt: As explained above, we have identified risk domains where, based on early research, we have determined significant or severe risks may be most likely to arise from future models: CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, as well as machine learning R&D and misalignment.
paraphrase: Four risk domains—CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, and ML R&D/misalignment—have been identified as most likely sources of significant or severe risk in future models.

excerpt: As part of our broader research into and development of frontier AI models, we continue to assess whether there are other risk domains where significant or severe risks may arise and will update our approach as appropriate.
paraphrase: Ongoing research assesses whether additional risk domains exist, with the approach to be updated as appropriate.

excerpt: For each of the four identified domains, we have developed specific scenarios and T/CCLs in which these risks could materialize.
paraphrase: Specific scenarios and T/CCLs have been developed for each of the four identified risk domains.

excerpt: To understand whether a model may, without appropriate mitigations, contribute to the risks identified, we conduct a closer assessment of its capabilities against the T/CCLs.
paraphrase: A closer capability assessment against T/CCLs is conducted to determine whether a model, absent mitigations, could contribute to identified risks.

excerpt: We conduct a critical capability assessment prior to the first external deployment of a new frontier AI model.
paraphrase: A critical capability assessment is conducted before first external deployment of a new frontier model.

excerpt: For external deployment of subsequent versions of the model, we determine whether a substantial modification has been made and whether a further critical capability assessment is required if (1) the model has meaningful new capabilities or material increases in performance; and (2) we believe such material capability increase could materially undermine the justification for why the risks stemming from the model are acceptable.
paraphrase: For later model versions, a further critical capability assessment is required if the model has meaningful new capabilities or performance gains that could undermine the risk-acceptability justification.

excerpt: To understand if a subsequent version of the model has meaningful new capabilities or material increases in performance relative to the last checkpoint subject to a critical capability assessment, we conduct material capability change assessments on various checkpoints upon the completion of a post-training run.
paraphrase: Material capability change assessments are conducted on checkpoints after post-training to compare against the last assessed checkpoint.

excerpt: These assessments draw on model characteristics, such as its provenance, size, modality, and performance on general capability benchmarks.
paraphrase: The assessments use model characteristics including provenance, size, modality, and general benchmark performance.

excerpt: To understand if such a change in capability in the subsequent version of the model could materially undermine the justification for why the risks stemming from the model are acceptable, we may also conduct light-weight versions of our “early warning evaluations” described below, including our automated benchmarks, to confirm a model remains below T/CCL.
paraphrase: Lightweight early warning evaluations, including automated benchmarks, may also be run to confirm a model stays below T/CCL.

excerpt: We may also apply material capability change assessments to models not on the frontier, to understand whether a critical capability assessment is required.
paraphrase: Material capability change assessments may also be applied to non-frontier models to determine if a critical capability assessment is needed.

excerpt: Central to our critical capability assessments are “early warning evaluations,” which we use to test the specific threats and risk scenarios identified through our threat modeling, determine a model’s capability, and assess the proximity of the model to a T/CCL.
paraphrase: Early warning evaluations are central to critical capability assessments, testing threat scenarios and gauging proximity to T/CCLs.

excerpt: For CCLs, we define “alert thresholds,” which may draw on evaluation results, expert assessments, and other sources of information; that are designed to flag when a CCL may be reached before a critical capability assessment is conducted again.
paraphrase: Alert thresholds are defined for CCLs to flag possible CCL attainment before the next critical capability assessment.

excerpt: In our evaluations, we seek to apply appropriate scaffolding, inference compute, and other augmentations to also assess the capabilities of systems that will likely be produced with the model based on the specific threats and risk scenarios we have identified for the T/CCL.
paraphrase: Evaluations aim to apply scaffolding, inference compute, and other augmentations to assess capabilities of systems likely built with the model.

excerpt: We may run early warning evaluations more frequently or adjust alert thresholds if the rate of progress suggests our safety buffer is no longer adequate.
paraphrase: Evaluation frequency may increase or alert thresholds may be adjusted if progress suggests the safety buffer is inadequate.

excerpt: We conduct further analysis, including reviewing model-independent information, external evaluations, and post-market monitoring as appropriate.
paraphrase: Further analysis, including model-independent information, external evaluations, and post-market monitoring, is conducted as appropriate.

excerpt: In particular, we strive to learn from our post-market monitoring mechanisms, including as part of our detection, mitigation, response and/or reporting of incidents relating to our frontier safety risk domains.
paraphrase: Post-market monitoring mechanisms, tied to incident detection, mitigation, response, and reporting, inform learning efforts.

excerpt: Actionable insights from these processes allow us to enhance our tools, training, processes, policies, and response efforts.
paraphrase: Insights from these processes are used to improve tools, training, processes, policies, and response efforts.

excerpt: Our approach to model evaluations and inherent risk assessments described above means we can proactively monitor a model’s capabilities throughout the entire lifecycle of the model and ensure that any significant or severe risk is properly identified and mitigated.
paraphrase: The evaluation and assessment approach enables proactive monitoring of a model's capabilities across its lifecycle and proper identification and mitigation of significant or severe risks.

excerpt: Where appropriate, we may engage relevant external actors, including governments, to inform our responsible development and deployment practices.
paraphrase: External actors, including governments, may be engaged where appropriate to inform responsible development and deployment.

excerpt: Note on Machine Learning R&D CCLs: Risk assessment must take into account the fact that other actors may put significantly more effort into eliciting capabilities than we put into assessing risk, thus requiring conservatism in the form of evaluations.
paraphrase: For ML R&D CCLs, risk assessment must account for the possibility that others invest more effort eliciting capabilities than is invested assessing risk, requiring conservative evaluations.

excerpt: However, as a frontier AI company, we do not expect other groups to put significantly more effort into ML R&D than we do ourselves.
paraphrase: As a frontier AI company, it is not expected that other groups invest significantly more in ML R&D than the company itself.

excerpt: As a result, to assess the ML R&D CCLs, we may use sources of information about our own progress at accelerating ML R&D to assess whether we are near or at the ML R&D CCLs, in addition to evaluations of ML R&D capabilities.
paraphrase: To assess ML R&D CCLs, information about the company's own progress accelerating ML R&D may be used alongside capability evaluations to determine proximity to the CCLs.

excerpt: We apply safety and security mitigations throughout the lifecycle of our models, including as part of our training and model development phase and, where appropriate, before T/CCLs are reached as described in the process below.
paraphrase: Safety and security mitigations are applied throughout the model lifecycle, including during training/development and, where appropriate, before T/CCLs are reached.

excerpt: When a model reaches an alert threshold for a CCL, we will assess the proximity of the model to the CCL and analyze the risk posed, involving internal and external experts as needed.
paraphrase: Upon reaching a CCL alert threshold, the model's proximity to the CCL and the posed risk will be assessed, involving experts as needed.

excerpt: This will inform the formulation and application of a response plan.
paraphrase: The assessment informs the formulation and application of a response plan.

excerpt: Central to most response plans will be the application of the mitigations described later in the Framework.
paraphrase: Response plans will mostly center on applying mitigations described later in the document.

excerpt: However, if we assess that risks stemming from the model remain acceptable and model capabilities remain distant from a CCL, the response plan may include updating the alert threshold to ensure the safety buffer remains appropriate.
paraphrase: If risks remain acceptable and capabilities remain distant from a CCL, the response plan may instead update the alert threshold to preserve an adequate safety buffer.

excerpt: We have two categories of mitigations: security mitigations (such as preventing the exfiltration of model weights), and deployment mitigations (such as safety fine-tuning and monitoring and response) intended to counter the misuse or misaligned expression of critical capabilities in deployments.
paraphrase: Mitigations fall into two categories: security mitigations (e.g., preventing weight exfiltration) and deployment mitigations (e.g., safety fine-tuning, monitoring, and response) countering misuse or misaligned expression of critical capabilities.

excerpt: The mitigations described in this document are limited to those mitigations that will be required to bring a model to an acceptable level of risk relative just to the specific T/CCL, which by definition pose the greatest risks of harm.
paraphrase: Described mitigations are limited to those needed to bring risk to an acceptable level relative specifically to the T/CCL, which represents the greatest harm risk.

excerpt: Because we cannot always anticipate what security and deployment mitigations will be appropriate for models beyond the current frontier, the specific mitigations we implement may be determined when a T/CCL is reached, informed by the threat landscape at that time.
paraphrase: Since appropriate mitigations for future models cannot always be foreseen, specific mitigations may be decided once a T/CCL is reached, based on the contemporary threat landscape.

excerpt: These mitigations also reflect considerations from the perspective of addressing significant and severe risks from powerful capabilities alone; due to this focused scope, other risk management and security considerations may result in more stringent mitigations applied to a model than specified by the Framework.
paraphrase: Because the Framework's mitigations focus solely on significant/severe risk from powerful capabilities, other considerations may lead to stricter mitigations than the Framework specifies.

excerpt: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
paraphrase: Lead-in stating various processes will be used to evaluate mitigation effectiveness and limitations.

context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
excerpt: Security mitigations: security infrastructure at Google is subject to penetration testing and other kinds of assessments, and is continually improved based on these results.
paraphrase: Google's security infrastructure undergoes penetration testing and other assessments, with continual improvement based on results.

context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
excerpt: Deployment mitigations: we will use a combination of threat modeling, empirical testing, and other sources of information to assess the effectiveness and limitations of our deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigation effectiveness and limitations will be assessed via threat modeling, empirical testing, and other information sources.

excerpt: Models reaching TCLs or CCLs will be subject to residual risk assessments as part of evaluating their deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: Models reaching TCLs or CCLs undergo residual risk assessments when evaluating deployment mitigations.

excerpt: For models reaching CCLs, the residual risk assessment will be informed by a supplemental safety case.
paraphrase: For models reaching CCLs, a supplemental safety case informs the residual risk assessment.

excerpt: See the deployment mitigations sections below regarding misuse and machine learning R&D and misalignment for more.
paraphrase: Further detail is available in the deployment mitigations sections on misuse and ML R&D/misalignment.

excerpt: The Framework outlines the risk acceptance determination approach for different model risks and capabilities pertaining to significant and severe risks.
paraphrase: The Framework sets out the risk acceptance determination approach across different model risks and capabilities.

excerpt: A model for which inherent risk assessment indicates no T/CCL is reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development and deployment, because it should not possess the capabilities required to substantially contribute to significant or severe risk scenarios.
paraphrase: A model assessed as not reaching any T/CCL is deemed acceptable risk for further development and deployment, since it lacks capabilities substantially contributing to significant or severe risk.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a misuse T/CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: We assess that the deployment mitigations have brought the residual risk of harm to an acceptable level, based on considerations such as the effectiveness of mitigations, the scope of the deployment, what capabilities and mitigations are available on other publicly available models (e.g. if other models are similarly capable and have few mitigations, then the marginal risk added by our external deployment is likely low), and the historical incidence and severity of related events.
paraphrase: One condition is that deployment mitigations must be assessed as reducing residual harm risk to an acceptable level, based on mitigation effectiveness, deployment scope, comparable mitigations on other public models, and historical incident severity.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a misuse T/CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if: [condition on deployment mitigations]
excerpt: This is required only for external deployment, not internal deployment or further development.
paraphrase: This deployment-mitigation condition applies only to external deployment, not internal deployment or further development.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a misuse T/CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: Security mitigations have been applied to the model weights reaching the recommended security level stated below, or we otherwise assess that the level of security applied is adequate, e.g. based on mitigations already in place, if they match or exceed the level of security applied to other models with similar capabilities or risk profiles, or we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Another condition is that security mitigations reach the recommended security level, or security is otherwise assessed adequate (e.g., matching comparable models), or the benefits of open weight release are judged to outweigh the risks.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a ML R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: We assess that the deployment mitigations have brought the residual risk of severe harm to an acceptable level, based on considerations such as the effectiveness of mitigations, and information pertaining to model propensities and the severity of related events.
paraphrase: For ML R&D CCLs, one condition is that deployment mitigations are assessed to bring residual severe-harm risk to an acceptable level, based on mitigation effectiveness and model propensity/severity information.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a ML R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if: [condition on deployment mitigations]
excerpt: This is required only for external deployment and high-risk internal deployment, not further development.
paraphrase: This ML R&D CCL condition applies only to external deployment and high-risk internal deployment, not further development.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates a ML R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: Security mitigations have been applied to the model weights reaching the recommended security level stated below, or we otherwise assess that the level of security applied is adequate, e.g. based on mitigations already in place, if they match or exceed the level of security applied to other models with similar capabilities or risk profiles, or we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Another ML R&D CCL condition is that security mitigations reach the recommended level, or are otherwise assessed adequate, or open weight release benefits are judged to outweigh risks.

excerpt: Note that deployment mitigations for the ML R&D CCLs are different than those for the misuse CCLs because of differences in which deployment could lead to severe harm for those respective categories.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigations differ between ML R&D CCLs and misuse CCLs because harm-causing deployment pathways differ between the two categories.

excerpt: In contrast, security mitigations protecting against weights exfiltration and unauthorized modification are generally beneficial to both kinds of risk.
paraphrase: Security mitigations against weight exfiltration and unauthorized modification generally benefit both risk categories.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates the TCL for ML R&D and misalignment risk has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: We assess that the deployment mitigations have brought the residual risk of significant harm to an acceptable level, based on considerations such as the effectiveness of mitigations, and information pertaining to model propensities and the severity of related events, or if we assess that the model is very unlikely to possess the propensities that would be required for material risk of significant harm through misalignment risk.
paraphrase: For the ML R&D/misalignment TCL, one condition is that deployment mitigations bring residual significant-harm risk to an acceptable level, or that the model is assessed very unlikely to possess propensities required for material misalignment harm.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates the TCL for ML R&D and misalignment risk has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if: [condition on deployment mitigations]
excerpt: This is required only for external deployment and high-risk internal deployment, not further development.
paraphrase: This TCL condition applies only to external deployment and high-risk internal deployment, not further development.

context_stem: A model for which the inherent risk assessment indicates the TCL for ML R&D and misalignment risk has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of residual risk for further development or deployment, if:
excerpt: We assess that the level of security applied is adequate, e.g. based on mitigations already in place, if they match or exceed the level of security applied to other models with similar capabilities or risk profiles, or we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Another TCL condition is that the level of security applied is assessed adequate, or that open weight release benefits are judged to outweigh the risks.

excerpt: Note: Assessing frontier AI capabilities and corresponding significant and severe risk is a complex process.
paraphrase: Assessing frontier AI capabilities and corresponding risk is described as a complex process.

excerpt: Because the science of AI risk assessment is still developing, our assessments will often involve some level of subjective analysis.
paraphrase: Because AI risk assessment science is still developing, assessments often involve subjective analysis.

excerpt: The concept of proportionality is central to our determination of whether a particular mitigation has sufficiently reduced the risk to acceptable levels.
paraphrase: Proportionality is central to determining whether a mitigation has sufficiently reduced risk to an acceptable level.

excerpt: The mitigation and the effects of such mitigation should also be assessed holistically and be proportionate with expected impact of a model’s risk, thus balancing safety with innovation.
paraphrase: Mitigations and their effects should be assessed holistically and proportionately to a model's expected risk impact, balancing safety with innovation.

excerpt: This section describes our mitigation approach for models that pose risks of significant or severe harm through misuse, and then details our set of misuse T/CCLs (CBRN, cyber and harmful manipulation), as well as the mitigation approach that we assess as appropriate for them.
paraphrase: The section introduces the mitigation approach for misuse-related risks and details the CBRN, cyber, and harmful manipulation T/CCLs and their mitigations.

excerpt: There are two categories of mitigations to address models with misuse critical capabilities: security mitigations intended to prevent the exfiltration or unauthorized modification of model weights, and deployment mitigations intended to counter the misuse of critical capabilities in external deployments.
paraphrase: Two mitigation categories address misuse critical capabilities: security mitigations against weight exfiltration/modification, and deployment mitigations against misuse in external deployment.

excerpt: For security, we have several levels of mitigations, allowing calibration of the appropriateness and robustness of security measures to the risks posed.
paraphrase: Several security mitigation levels allow calibrating measure robustness to the posed risk.

excerpt: Regarding deployment mitigations for models reaching T/CCLs, we specify a standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing mitigations: the aim of this process is to calibrate mitigations to T/CCLs, and the procedural approach reflects the more iterative and T/CCL-dependent nature of deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: A standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing deployment mitigations calibrates them to T/CCLs, reflecting their iterative, T/CCL-dependent nature.

excerpt: This structured process for deployment mitigations is centered on assessing and reviewing that the risk of severe harm has been brought to an acceptable level proportionate to the risk.
paraphrase: The structured deployment mitigation process centers on confirming that severe harm risk has been reduced to a proportionate acceptable level.

excerpt: Security mitigations against exfiltration or unauthorized modification risk, such as identity and access management practices and hardening interface-access to unreleased model parameters, are important for models reaching misuse CCLs.
paraphrase: Security mitigations like access management and hardened interface access are important for models reaching misuse CCLs.

excerpt: This is because the release or unauthorized modification of model weights may enable the removal of any safeguards trained into or deployed with the model, and hence access (including by threat actors) to any critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Weight release or unauthorized modification could remove trained safeguards and expose critical capabilities, including to threat actors.

excerpt: Using Google’s Secure AI Framework (SAIF) and Google’s common security infrastructure, we implement state-of-the-art security mitigations.
paraphrase: State-of-the-art security mitigations are implemented using Google's SAIF and common security infrastructure.

excerpt: SAIF is a defense-in-depth approach that embeds security into every layer of our AI systems—from data and infrastructure to models and applications.
paraphrase: SAIF is a defense-in-depth approach embedding security across all AI system layers.

excerpt: SAIF is premised on six core elements: strong security foundations, detection and response, automated defenses, harmonized platform-level controls, adaptable controls to mitigate emerging threats, and end-to-end risk assessments.
paraphrase: SAIF rests on six core elements including security foundations, detection/response, automated defenses, platform-level controls, adaptable threat controls, and end-to-end risk assessments.

excerpt: We use security levels to indicate security goals/principles in line with the corresponding level in the RAND model weight security framework.
paraphrase: Security levels indicate goals/principles aligned with corresponding levels in RAND's model weight security framework.

excerpt: We also define and recommend "Security Level 2+," which uses RAND Security Level 2 (SL2) as a baseline, with additional security measures designed to address risks from insider threats and well-resourced non-state external actors.
paraphrase: "Security Level 2+" is defined and recommended, using RAND SL2 as baseline plus additional measures for insider threats and well-resourced non-state actors.

excerpt: These additional measures may include, for example: dedicated insider risk teams; background checks and ID verification for personnel with sensitive access; review of model training data for signs of tampering; mandating that the processing of untrusted inputs occurs within sandboxed environments; advanced red-teaming that simulates well-resourced adversaries (including Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups); and proactive threat hunting with 24/7 incident response capabilities.
paraphrase: Examples of additional measures include dedicated insider risk teams, background checks/ID verification, training data tampering review, sandboxed processing of untrusted inputs, advanced red-teaming against APT-level adversaries, and 24/7 proactive threat hunting and incident response.

excerpt: Because AI security is an area of active research, we expect the concrete measures implemented to reach each level of security to evolve substantially.
paraphrase: As AI security research is active, the concrete measures used to achieve each security level are expected to evolve substantially.

excerpt: In other words, “security level N” indicates security controls and detections at a level generally aligned with RAND SL N.
paraphrase: The footnote clarifies that "security level N" means controls generally aligned with RAND SL N.

excerpt: See https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html, pp 21-22.
paraphrase: A citation to the RAND report pages 21-22 is provided.

excerpt: In aligning our security levels with RAND’s, we are referring to the security goals and principles in the RAND framework, rather than the benchmarks (i.e. concrete measures) also described in the RAND report.
paraphrase: Alignment with RAND levels refers to RAND's goals and principles, not its specific benchmark measures.

excerpt: As the authors point out, the “security level benchmarks represent neither a complete standard nor a compliance regime—they are provided for informational purposes only and should inform security teams’ decisions rather than supersede them.”
paraphrase: The footnote quotes RAND authors stating the security level benchmarks are informational only, not a complete standard or compliance regime.
